facts.value: Proteins provide the building blocks for many of the structural elements of the body, such as muscle, as well as functional molecules such as hormones and enzymes.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: Protein intake at 10–15% of total daily energy intake is generally sufficient to meet the needs of adults (approximately 50–75 grams for a person of healthy body weight consuming about 2000 calories per day).
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: Protein intake may be greater than 15% of total daily energy intake during adolescence, and for athletes, body builders and others actively building and/or maintaining significant amounts of muscle mass.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: Consuming excessive amounts of protein, however, can place a metabolic burden on the body, particularly the kidneys.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: Protein can come from a mix of animal and plant sources.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: Protein digestibility and quality should also be considered, particularly in childhood and adolescence.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: In some contexts, switching to more plant-based sources of protein may be preferable to decrease risk of diet-related noncommunicable diseases in adults.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree

facts.value: In other contexts, consumption of animal source foods is still important to favour nutrient intakes, particularly in children and pregnant/lactating women.
facts.programme_association: Healthy Lifestyles and Fitness Science Degree
